clue.text: Space not to be confused with one of one's own

definitions.text: Space not to be confused with one of one's own

parts.words: Space not to be confused with one of one's own
parts.note: Virginia Woolf wrote both a novel named after a man's chamber and the essay 'A Room of One's Own'; the clue asks for the one that is not the essay

explanation.surface: A warning not to mistake a shared space for a private one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One's own' points to Woolf's essay; the answer is her 1922 novel, another room by the same author.
explanation.definitionFit: Woolf's novel is titled after a young man's lodging, so it is a literary space distinct from her famous essay.

clue.text: Leo Rosten happily shared those of yiddish

definitions.text: Leo Rosten happily shared those of yiddish

parts.words: Leo Rosten happily shared those of yiddish
parts.note: Leo Rosten wrote a celebrated 1968 lexicon whose title names the delights of the Yiddish language; 'happily' hints at the pleasure in that title

explanation.surface: A writer cheerfully passes on the treasures of a language.
explanation.definitionFit: Rosten's book is 'The --- of Yiddish', delights or pleasures being what he shared.

clue.text: Old Fabian King?

parts.note: G. D. H. ... was an early Fabian socialist, and the nursery rhyme monarch is Old King ---, so one surname fits both

explanation.surface: Was there a veteran monarch of the Fabian Society?
explanation.walkthrough: The Fabian Society is a British socialist group; G. D. H. Cole was a leading member. 'Old King Cole' is the merry monarch of a nursery rhyme.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname belongs both to the Fabian economist G. D. H. Cole and to the nursery rhyme's merry old monarch.

clue.text: Dowling boded no good in Lorca piece

indicators.note: something no good is spoiled or broken, so the letters are scrambled into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone named Dowling foresaw disaster in a Spanish play.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no good' looks like what Dowling foretold, but it signals an anagram of DOWLING BODED.
explanation.definitionFit: Federico García Lorca's 1932 tragedy of a fatal marriage is this play, his best-known stage work.

clue.text: Switched-on type in Capek piece

parts.note: Karel Čapek's play R.U.R. introduced the artificial workers that one literally switches on; 'switched-on' also means alert and trendy

explanation.surface: A bright, up-to-date character in a Czech play.
explanation.walkthrough: Čapek's 1920 play R.U.R. gave the world the word for a mechanical worker; 'switched-on' is read literally, as powered up.
explanation.definitionFit: Čapek coined the term for a manufactured artificial worker, a machine that must be powered on.

clue.text: They all informed against Hamlet, spurring his revenge

definitions.text: They all informed against Hamlet, spurring his revenge

parts.words: They all informed against Hamlet, spurring his revenge
parts.note: Hamlet's soliloquy begins 'How all --- do inform against me, And spur my dull revenge'

explanation.surface: A group of informers betrayed the prince and drove him to vengeance.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue paraphrases Hamlet, Act 4 Scene 4: the events and circumstances around him reproach his delay.
explanation.definitionFit: In the soliloquy, events or circumstances are what reproach the prince and urge on his vengeance.

clue.text: He appears in some wild story, they say, about a ghost

definitions.text: He appears in some wild story, they say, about a ghost

parts.words: He appears in some wild story, they say, about a ghost
parts.note: 'wild', said out loud, gives Wilde; his story The Canterville Ghost features the American minister Hiram B. ... and his family

explanation.surface: A man features in an outlandish tale reportedly concerning a spook.
explanation.walkthrough: 'they say' turns 'wild' into Oscar Wilde, whose The Canterville Ghost has an American family who buy a haunted English house.
explanation.definitionFit: Hiram B. Otis is the American diplomat who buys the haunted house in Wilde's comic ghost story.

clue.text: Cut scene of Jelly Roll Morton's early success

definitions.meaning: a cut of meat, the tender strip of beef or pork beneath the ribs

definitions.text: scene of Jelly Roll Morton's early success
definitions.meaning: a red-light district (of San Francisco and New York) where jazz players such as Jelly Roll Morton played

explanation.surface: A jazz pianist's breakthrough is edited out of a film.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a choice cut of beef and the vice district where early jazz pianists found work.

clue.text: A visit … which the squire made on his horse with a pair of ——' containing his wardrobe " (Thomas Hughes)

definitions.text: A visit … which the squire made on his horse with a pair of ——' containing his wardrobe " (Thomas Hughes)

parts.words: A visit … which the squire made on his horse with a pair of ——' containing his wardrobe
parts.note: a quotation from Tom Brown's Schooldays: the gap is the pair of bags slung over a horse to carry a rider's clothes

explanation.surface: A squire rides out on a visit with his clothes packed on his horse.
explanation.definitionFit: Pouches hung in pairs across a horse behind the seat carry luggage, here the squire's clothes.

clue.text: Cowardly defender of cheap edition

parts.note: yellow is slang for cowardly
a back is a defending player in football or rugby

explanation.surface: A timid footballer protects a bargain book.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'yellowback' was a cheap Victorian novel in yellow boards, sold at railway stalls.
explanation.definitionFit: Victorian railway-stall fiction came in inexpensive yellow board covers, giving its name to that kind of cheap book.

clue.text: Seen with Miss Bagnold, returning to eat

indicators.note: returning means the word for eating is read backwards

parts.note: to dine is to eat a meal

explanation.surface: Someone is spotted with a novelist, coming back for dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returning' turns DINE back to front.
explanation.definitionFit: Enid Bagnold, author of National Velvet, was the novelist's first name.

clue.text: "A good editor is a man … who has a — on my publisher" (John Cheever)

definitions.text: "A good editor is a man … who has a — on my publisher" (John Cheever)

parts.words: A good editor is a man … who has a — on my publisher
parts.note: John Cheever's quip: the gap is a wrestling grip that throttles, a tight power over his publisher

explanation.surface: A novelist praises an editor who can force a publisher's hand.
explanation.definitionFit: A grip on the throat in wrestling, figuratively complete control over someone.

clue.text: Poet is careless well edit this

indicators.note: careless work is jumbled, so the letters fall into a different order

explanation.surface: A slapdash poet is told to edit this text properly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'careless' signals an anagram of WELL EDIT THIS.
explanation.definitionFit: Edith Sitwell was an English modernist poet, author of Façade.

clue.text: Half a dozen of them looking for Pirandello?

definitions.text: Half a dozen of them looking for Pirandello?

parts.words: Half a dozen of them looking for Pirandello?
parts.note: Pirandello's play is 'Six --- in Search of an Author', and Pirandello himself is that author

explanation.surface: Six people are hunting for an Italian dramatist.
explanation.walkthrough: Half a dozen is six; Pirandello's play has six figures searching for a writer to finish their story.
explanation.definitionFit: Stage figures or roles in a drama, six of them in Pirandello's play.

clue.text: Married woman, superb that is as bishop's wife

parts.note: Mrs is the title of a married woman
proud can mean splendid or superb, as in a proud ship
i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is

explanation.surface: A married woman, magnificent, as befits a bishop's spouse.
explanation.walkthrough: Mrs Proudie is the domineering wife of Bishop Proudie in Trollope's Barchester novels.
explanation.definitionFit: Trollope's Barchester novels give Bishop Proudie a formidable spouse who rules the diocese.

clue.text: He pressed his suit with white Italian girl in Padua

definitions.text: He pressed his suit with white Italian girl in Padua

parts.words: He pressed his suit with white Italian girl in Padua
parts.note: in The Taming of the Shrew, set in Padua, one suitor of Bianca (Italian for white) woos her disguised as a music teacher

explanation.surface: A man ironed his suit alongside a pale Italian girl in Padua.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pressed his suit' means wooed, not ironed; 'white Italian girl' is Bianca, whose name is Italian for white.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Shrew has Bianca courted by several men in Padua; this one disguises himself as her music tutor.

clue.text: He pants, that is odd, for Alan Paton's neurotic aunt

indicators.note: something odd is strange or out of order, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: i.e. is the abbreviation of id est, that is

explanation.surface: A man gasps strangely about a South African novelist's nervous relative.
explanation.walkthrough: 'odd' rearranges HE PANTS into STEPHAN, and IE follows. The aunt is in Paton's Too Late the Phalarope.
explanation.definitionFit: Alan Paton's novel Too Late the Phalarope gives the narrator this name, an anxious aunt.

clue.text: It came from the performer's cuff

definitions.text: It came from the performer's cuff

parts.words: It came from the performer's cuff
parts.note: something said 'off the cuff' is unprepared; a performer's unscripted line is meant

explanation.surface: Something emerged from an entertainer's sleeve.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Off the cuff' means improvised, so the performer's line is unscripted.
explanation.definitionFit: An improvised remark or line spoken without a script, Latin for 'at pleasure'.

clue.text: "This particularly—, unintelligible patter" (W. S. Gilbert)

parts.note: from the Matter Patter trio in Gilbert and Sullivan's Ruddigore: the gap describes very fast speech

explanation.surface: A line of Gilbert's lyric about patter too fast to follow.
explanation.definitionFit: Very fast, as patter delivered at speed in comic opera.

clue.text: Casual departure of Marryat hero?

parts.note: Captain Marryat's novel Mr Midshipman Easy has Jack Easy as its hero
going is leaving, a departure

explanation.surface: A relaxed farewell to a seafaring novel's hero.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'departure of Marryat hero' as Easy going.
explanation.definitionFit: Relaxed and unconcerned, an informal temperament.

clue.text: Unreliable counsel shows 12 verses

indicators.note: unreliable advice cannot be trusted to stay in shape, so the letters are reordered

explanation.surface: Untrustworthy advice is put on display.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unreliable' signals an anagram of COUNSEL SHOWS. '12' is 12 across: Clowns' Houses (1918) is a collection by that poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Edith Sitwell's 1918 poetry collection, so a book of poems by the 12-across poet.

clue.text: The world of Reginald Hill

parts.note: Reginald Hill wrote a Dalziel and Pascoe novel titled with the criminal or mining world beneath the surface; the light gives its first half

explanation.surface: A crime writer's fictional universe.
explanation.walkthrough: Hill's 1988 novel Underworld is set in a mining village; the light is the word before 'world'.
explanation.definitionFit: Reginald Hill's novel title is completed by 'world', making the criminal milieu below the surface.

clue.text: Strange case of a rune

indicators.note: strange means odd or altered, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An odd example of a runic letter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strange' signals an anagram of CASE.
explanation.definitionFit: Æsc, meaning ash tree, is the Old English runic letter for the æ sound.

clue.text: Poet of the riverbank

definitions.meaning: Henry ..., author of the war poem 'Naming of Parts'
a tall waterside grass that grows on riverbanks

explanation.surface: A versifier who lives by the river.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry Reed was an English poet, and the same word is a tall grass growing at the water's edge.

clue.text: Mythological stories from collected Danish lore

indicators.note: from shows that the letters are taken out of the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: Myths gathered from a store of Scandinavian legend.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' points inside 'collectED DAnish'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Old Norse collections of poems and prose on gods and heroes bear this name.

clue.text: Emergent Olympian swimmer

parts.note: Aphrodite, an Olympian goddess, is painted rising from the sea foam under the Greek epithet meaning rising up

explanation.surface: A competitor at the Olympics climbs out of the pool.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Olympian' means a god on Mount Olympus, not an athlete; Aphrodite born from the sea is given the epithet 'rising from the sea'.
explanation.definitionFit: A Greek epithet of Aphrodite as she rises from the waves, a sea-born goddess.

clue.text: Unwillingly introduce that of Pearl Buck

definitions.text: Unwillingly introduce that of Pearl Buck

parts.words: Unwillingly introduce that of Pearl Buck
parts.note: Pearl Buck's novel is Dragon ---; 'unwillingly introduce' suggests 'drag on', the first part of that title

explanation.surface: Someone reluctantly brings in a novel by an American author.
explanation.walkthrough: To introduce unwillingly is to 'drag on'; Pearl Buck's 1942 novel is Dragon Seed.
explanation.definitionFit: The word completes Pearl Buck's title Dragon Seed, the 'dragon' part being 'drag on'.

clue.text: Printed conceivably proud creed

indicators.note: conceivably means possibly, as in a possible rearrangement of the letters that follow

explanation.surface: A belief held with pride, perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'conceivably' signals an anagram of PROUD CREED, and hints at breeding, another sense of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Copied in print, as a picture or text is run off again.
